item.title: In A.I. Race, U.S. Models Have the Edge, but China Has Other Advantages
item.description:
There is no shortage of issues on the table for possible discussion as President Trump prepares to welcome the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, for a state visit beginning Wednesday evening, including the Iran war, Taiwan and tariffs.

But no topic has captured global fascination in recent weeks more than whether the two sides can reach any agreements around the pace of artificial intelligence development. The rapidly shifting debate about the risks of A.I. has so consumed Silicon Valley, Washington and, in recent days, the United Nations that some observers have likened the U.S.-China summit to a Cold War tête-à-tête during the nuclear arms race.

Though some see the stakes this week as nothing short of civilizational, the expectations for any serious accord remain low. The countries are locked in an A.I. race that both sides see as decisive to gaining the upper hand militarily, technologically and economically, and mutual suspicion runs deep, according to foreign policy analysts.

Western experts generally estimate that the United States is somewhere around six months ahead of China in the A.I. race when it comes to its leading models. But that figure obscures the complex relationship between the two nations, further complicating efforts to reach agreement on how to address A.I. safety risks.

Here is a look at where the United States has the upper hand against China on A.I. and where it is lagging behind its top geopolitical rival.

The United States has one undeniable advantage over China: computer chips. Most of the specialized chips used to build and operate A.I. technologies are designed by American companies. This includes the Silicon Valley chipmaker Nvidia, which is now the world’s most valuable company.

“The people who have made the fastest chips are here,” said Andrew Feldman, the chief executive of the Silicon Valley chipmaker Cerebras. “And they are not in China.”

Over the past decade, three American presidential administrations have imposed export controls that limited Chinese access to powerful chips. Even as China works to evade these controls, Chinese A.I. researchers often say that chip shortages are the biggest obstacle they face.

The leading Chinese companies have spent hundreds of millions of dollars to secure the chips they need. To bypass American export controls, they often buy remote access to data centers outside of China. Over the past year, this allowed China to shrink the performance gap between its systems and the leading American technologies.

At the same, China is working to build its own chip-making industry. But by its own admission, Huawei, the telecommunications and electronics company that leads this effort, is still years away from producing chips that perform as well as those offered by Nvidia today.

Chinese A.I. companies say they are already using chips from Huawei, but these chips are unlikely to provide much help in building cutting-edge technologies. Less-powerful chips are typically used to serve technologies to users across the internet.

Even with help from Huawei, Chinese A.I. companies like Moonshot have struggled to find the additional chips they need to meet demand.

Public polling in the United States shows that A.I. has become increasingly unpopular over the past year — so much so that it has now become a key issue in the midterm elections. Many Americans are worried about A.I. threatening their jobs, undermining education and, more recently, posing a threat to humanity. A Pew Research Center poll this week found that 60 percent of Americans were uncomfortable with a new local data center.

Though Mr. Trump has dismissed calls for an A.I. slowdown as a “hoax,” a growing number of Republican and Democratic lawmakers, governors and 2028 presidential hopefuls are scrambling to offer a wide range of proposals seeking to regulate the technology after disclosures about rogue A.I. agents hacking into other companies.

By nature of its centralized systems, China does not need to contend with a boisterous public debate about how or whether to rein in A.I. And though polling in China can be dubious, surveys consistently point to more enthusiasm for its adoption.

Chinese citizens broadly appear to be much more optimistic about A.I. — and in fact are some of the most hopeful about the technology in the entire world, according to a KPMG survey of 47 countries last year. Some 69 percent of people in China said the technology’s benefits outweighed its risks, compared with just 35 percent of Americans who agreed. The technology is also more embedded in day-to-day life, including service robots in hotels and restaurants, as well as medical chatbots at hospitals.

Another advantage for the United States is that its economy has been more resilient during the A.I. boom. Stock indexes are near record highs, and worries of an A.I. bubble also have so far not materialized. Fears of job losses prompted by the technology proliferating throughout corporate America have yet to really appear in economic data.

There are some signs that A.I. is contributing to slower wage growth in jobs most exposed to the technology and fewer job openings, especially for young workers. And applying to jobs, especially for entry-level workers, has become even more daunting thanks to A.I. being used to either write résumés or screen applicants. But overall, the economic distress directly linked to A.I. has been far less than many economists predicted.

In China, the story is different. Its economic struggles, including high youth unemployment, consumer pullback on spending and a deflationary spiral, threaten to undercut Beijing’s vast investments in A.I. Chinese economists have recently issued warnings that the economy is vulnerable and potentially being made more precarious because of the country’s A.I.-centered allocation of spending.

In the United States, the leading artificial intelligence companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic, maintain tight control over how their technologies are used. They build elaborate guardrails, hoping to prevent users from spreading disinformation or hacking into computer networks.

As concern mounts over the risks of A.I., these companies are calling for federal regulations that would toughen this approach. They say the government should review their A.I. technologies before release to ensure that the proper guardrails are in place — and many policymakers, lawmakers and pundits agree.

But the leading Chinese companies take a different stance. Companies like DeepSeek, Moonshot and Z.ai typically make their most powerful technologies “open source,” meaning anyone is free to use and modify these systems as they see fit.

Open source has driven the development of computer software, the internet and artificial intelligence for decades. The idea is that technology advances faster when its computer code is freely available for anyone to examine, use and improve upon.

In open-sourcing their technologies, Chinese companies can essentially combine their resources and accelerate their efforts. And if U.S. regulators stifle the progress of American open-source projects — as some lawmakers are suggesting they should — China could gain a significant edge.

If the best open-source systems come from China, many experts contend, developers across the globe will build atop Chinese technologies. This is already starting to happen, even in Silicon Valley.

“These models are still rough around the edges, but there are tasks where they are on par with the leading American systems,” said Rehaan Ahmad, a co-founder of the Silicon Valley start-up alphaXiv, who has used the latest Chinese technologies for the past several months.

Anyone can use these open-source technologies for malicious purposes, including, most notably, cyberattacks. But security experts say this is balanced by another phenomenon: Anyone can use the same technologies to defend against malicious attacks.

Some believe that if China can build a viable chip industry, it could race ahead of the United States because of an advantage it has developed in another area: electrical power.

Packed into giant data centers by the thousands, the leading chips require enormous amounts of electricity. They need so much electrical power, the big U.S. companies cannot get what they need from the existing power grid. Increasingly, they are turning to wind power or nuclear or even gas turbines installed alongside their data centers.

“At a fundamental level, the tech industry is trying to convert electricity into intelligence,” said Mr. Feldman, the Cerebras chief executive. “It’s like a Dr. Seuss machine. In goes chips and power — and out comes intelligence.”

Although the United States has a significant edge in terms of chips, Mr. Feldman said, he believes that China could pull ahead because it has spent years rebuilding its electrical grid. “That is going to be a huge asset,” he said. “Our grid is 1950s technology.”

As far back as 2024, studies showed that by some metrics, China had eclipsed the United States as the biggest producer of A.I. talent, generating almost half of the world’s leading researchers. By comparison, only about 18 percent came from the United States.

Researchers born and educated in China have for years played major roles inside leading U.S. artificial intelligence labs. And as newer studies have shown, they continue to drive important A.I. research across American industry and academia. But a growing number of them now stay in China, working for companies like Moonshot, Z.ai and DeepSeek.

item.title: As Xi Visits Washington, Trump Plays Down China’s Actions Against U.S. Interests
item.description:
In the weeks leading up to President Trump welcoming President Xi Jinping of China to Washington on Wednesday evening, Beijing has been accused of undermining America’s national interests on a number of fronts.

Mr. Trump accused the country this summer of “sinister election meddling” in the 2020 election, a breach he considered so historic he presented the claims in a prime-time address. Since the start of the war with Iran, Chinese companies have provided Tehran with satellite imagery, and access to a spy satellite, that Iran’s military forces have used to mount attacks in the region, according to multiple U.S. officials. And Beijing has shown no signs of retreating from its business dealings with Iran, in defiance of U.S. efforts to cut off economic lifelines to Tehran.

But as his meeting with Mr. Xi approached, Mr. Trump has repeatedly found ways to give him a pass — portraying him more as a personal friend than as a geopolitical competitor despite significant rivalries on matters of global power, trade, artificial intelligence and more.

Mr. Trump has spent weeks boosting the visit as a major event for the United States, sprucing up the White House beforehand, and planning for a state visit that will start with a rare greeting at Joint Base Andrews.

Even staunch allies of Mr. Trump have bristled at the plans.

On Tuesday, Senator Roger Wicker, Republican of Mississippi and chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said in a speech on the Senate floor that he would have advised against the invitation to the “brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America.”

Mr. Wicker said he hoped Mr. Trump would press Mr. Xi on “the purposes of China’s massive military buildup, or about China’s clear support for Iran.”

Responding to Mr. Wicker’s comments, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the visit reflected an acknowledgment by Mr. Trump that despite disagreements, China is one of the largest economic and military powers in the world.

“The relationship between the United States and China will define the 21st century, what happens in that relationship,” Mr. Rubio said. “The idea that we would not interact with them at the highest levels is irresponsible. It’s outrageous. We have to.”

Foreign policy experts say that Mr. Trump’s posture has been striking even for a president who prides himself on his personal brand of diplomacy.

“Trump is displaying an extraordinary degree of deference to Xi,” said Julian Gewirtz, a scholar at Columbia University who has written on the history of U.S.-China relations. “He is lavishing honors on China’s leader while downplaying threats to American interests. Beijing could scarcely have asked for a more accommodating host.”

Mr. Gewirtz, who also served a former White House and State Department official working on China under President Joseph R. Biden Jr., said that traditionally it has been Beijing that has sought out a state visit. This time, he said, the dynamic seems reversed. What Mr. Trump emerges with from all of the spectacle will be a test of his brand of diplomacy, which emphasizes personal ties.

“Washington has often leveraged symbolic honors to seek substantive gains from Beijing,” he said. “So the question is straightforward: What is Trump getting for America in return for all this ceremony?”

In a call with reporters, White House officials said the agenda with Mr. Xi will include topics like artificial intelligence, fentanyl and the upcoming expiration of a trade truce.

Asked whether the president planned to raise Mr. Trump’s allegations that China interfered in the 2020 election, the White House had no comment.

Another White House official pushed back against the premise that Mr. Trump was overly deferential to Mr. Xi. The official pointed to a number of measures the United States has taken that have affected China’s economy, including a marked decline on exports to the United States.

The person said the United States has targeted some entities that have been found to support Iran — though no major banks — and that other measures are in the works behind the scenes that have not yet been announced.

The officials spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the visit ahead of time.

(Last month, when Mr. Trump was asked why he was not targeting Chinese banks the way he was generally targeting allies like Canada, he snapped back: “Well, who said I’m not? You said, why not. I mean, who said I’m not. You don’t know if I’m doing it. Well, I don’t have to announce everything, do I?”)

A Treasury Department spokesman said in a follow-up email that Secretary Scott Bessent, who is spearheading the so-called “Operation Economic Outcast” operation, has made it clear to China that it will not hesitate to hold them accountable for supporting Iran economically.

In recent weeks, when pressed about China’s behavior, Mr. Trump at several points seemed to make excuses for Mr. Xi.

During an Oval Office event this month in which he called the war in Iran “small potatoes,” Mr. Trump suggested that China’s aid to Iran was negligible because of his personal plea.

“I said, please don’t get involved to President Xi — I have a very good relationship,” Mr. Trump said. “And they’re not really involved. Very little involvement by China. China could have plenty of involvement. They get 50 percent of the oil from the Hormuz strait.”

Later in the month, when asked about reports that Chinese entities may have provided the Iranians with satellite imagery that led to deadly strikes on U.S. forces in Jordan, again Mr. Trump demurred.

“They basically do what we do,” he said.

“Are you going to raise that with Xi when he visits?” a reporter asked.

“I think he’s behaved reasonably well, and we behave reasonably well,” Mr. Trump said. “You know when they say that China spies on us, I say you’re right, and we spy on them too. You know, we spy on them too.”

Pressed during a Fox News interview about what Mr. Xi may want from his visit, Mr. Trump pivoted to his consistent refrain: “You know, he and I get along very well.”

That the visit comes after Mr. Trump has spent weeks escalating attacks on America’s allies presents a particularly jarring split-screen, several foreign policy analysts say.

“There’s a rule of international politics that American presidents normally follow: treat your allies better than your adversaries,” said R. Nicholas Burns, the top U.S. diplomat in Beijing under the Biden administration. “And we don’t want to give the impression to our allies that we actually care more about this relationship with Xi Jinping than we care about the relationship with them. I think the president is giving that impression by being so unremittingly uncritical of the Chinese.”

Mr. Burns added that Mr. Trump’s tactics are unlikely to work on China, which he said responds to strength.

“They are practical, hardheaded, cynical about the United States,” Mr. Burns said. “They’re going to judge us, I think, by how strong we are and how much we push back when we have to push back. I think the Chinese understand power and deterrence. They’ll be swayed more and affected more by a strong American position than they will by flattery.”

If previous summits are any indication, Mr. Trump’s pageantry and flattery to impress Mr. Xi won’t go far, analysts say. When the two met in Korea last year to de-escalate a fierce trade war, for example, Mr. Trump did most of the talking and Mr. Xi stayed largely silent. Mr. Trump called Mr. Xi “a friend of mine” and called him “powerful.” The Chinese president approached the meeting with caution and steeliness. In his remarks, Mr. Xi likened China-U.S. relations to a “giant ship” that requires steady joint leadership.

The two leaders come to the U.S. summit in vastly different positions, said Jonathan A. Czin, a researcher at the Brookings Institution who previously worked at the C.I.A. analyzing Chinese politics.

Mr. Xi arrives with time on his side, hoping to buy more for relief from U.S. pressure, as he plans for a fourth term that will keep him in power for another five years. Mr. Trump is facing a midterm election in a few weeks where his policies where his party faces an uphill battle as a result of some of his policies.

“Xi is going to walk into this meeting and is going to be keenly aware of the fact that just weeks from now, Trump is in all likelihood going to be at best a lame-duck president, and at worst, he’s going to be politically maimed at home and have to deal with divided government,” Mr. Czin said.

He continued: “Xi is already thinking about ‘How am I going to keep this gentlemen’s agreement going with the United States,’ buying that time, and already thinking about what comes after Trump.”

Mr. Trump has long had an affinity for autocrats. He regularly boasts about his relationship with Russian President Vladimir Putin. This summer he trumpeted what he said was his good relationship with North Korea’s dictator, Kim Jong-un, while canceling long-running military exercises with South Korea, a U.S. ally.

Ruth Ben-Ghiat, a historian at New York University who studies fascism and authoritarianism, said that Mr. Trump has always admired Mr. Xi as having the kind of power he covets.

She pointed out that Mr. Trump’s doomsday declaration last month that “communism is the greatest threat to our country in its history,” had no bearing on Mr. Trump’s “fawning” over the leader of one of the powerful communist countries.

She also pointed to Mr. Trump’s latest defense of China’s government last week when a reporter raised that it was one of the most repressive countries in the world for journalists. Mr. Trump interrupted the reporter’s question, responding: “Well, I don’t know about that. I think we’re repressive also.” (That same day he would ban news organizations whose coverage he doesn’t like from the White House grounds).

“This meeting of head of states has importance for the optics it generates,” Ms. Ben-Ghiat said. “Two powerful strongmen, meeting as equals, at least in Trump’s mind — and for the potential for deals conducted in a nontransparent fashion.”

item.title: As Trump Welcomes Xi, More Americans Have a Positive View of China
item.description:
President Trump’s shift to a friendlier stance on China mirrors a startling change in public opinion. Across the political spectrum, more Americans are seeing China in a positive light.

Surveys from leading pollsters, including two released this week, show that China’s image in the United States has improved markedly in recent years. People are still skeptical about China, but as Mr. Trump prepares to give the country’s leader, Xi Jinping, a warm welcome in Washington this week, his accommodation echoes what some experts see as a desire among Americans for a more stable relationship with Beijing.

“There really is this warming toward China, even if on balance views still remain fairly negative,” said Laura Silver, an associate director at the Pew Research Center, which published survey data on Wednesday showing that 54 percent of Americans now have a “cold” view of China, compared to 68 percent in 2021.

The surveys do not pinpoint the reasons for the shift, which appears to be more pronounced among younger Americans. But experts point to fading memories of the coronavirus pandemic, awareness of China’s tech innovations and disaffection with Mr. Trump’s trade wars as contributing to a changing mood that could affect how U.S. politicians approach China.

The Chicago Council on Global Affairs, a think tank that has long studied the country’s foreign policy views, has picked up a reversal over just the last two years. By 2024, the share of Americans who favored “friendly cooperation and engagement with China” had declined to just 40 percent. But when the organization asked the question again this July, that number had risen to 57 percent, including 68 percent of Democrats and 43 percent of Republicans, according to data published this week.

“The attitudes toward China have been really surprising,” said Dina Smeltz, a former State Department official who oversees the Chicago Council’s polling. “They’ve shifted from a majority wanting to limit the rise of China and limit its influence to now a majority of Americans wanting to engage cooperatively with China.”

The research organization Gallup found earlier this year that the share of Americans with a favorable view of China had risen to 34 percent, more than double the low point in 2023.

The surveys all point to a changed national mood compared to a decade ago, when Mr. Trump’s harsh anti-China rhetoric helped define his winning presidential campaign. President Joseph R. Biden Jr. largely maintained and expanded Mr. Trump’s tough policies, including tariffs and export controls, cementing what appeared to be a bipartisan consensus that the United States needed to push back hard against China’s rise.

Now that consensus has weakened, as made plain by Mr. Trump himself. He stepped back last year from tariffs as high as 145 percent to pursue what has looked like an effort of reconciliation with China. It was on display in his deferential visit to Beijing in April and what is expected to be a lavish welcome for Mr. Xi this week — all without Beijing making major concessions on longstanding U.S. demands on trade or security issues.

The polls show that Republicans remain more hawkish on China than Democrats, though Republicans’ views of China have grown more positive as well — perhaps a reflection of Mr. Trump’s own shift. Despite the country’s polarization, Democrats have also moved in the same direction.

Just a year or two ago, politicians could “propose almost any kind of tough policy against China and the public would be behind it,” said Bruce Stokes, an expert on foreign policy polling at the German Marshall Fund, a think tank. “This public opinion data seems to suggest that support for a tough-on-China policy has weakened a little bit.”

Americans’ views of China, of course, could quickly shift again, especially amid fears of its artificial intelligence prowess and the risk of armed conflict over Taiwan. Pollsters note that Americans generally spend little time thinking about foreign policy and rarely let international issues determine how they vote.

But people who study the U.S. relationship with China see the polling figures as reflective of a changing geopolitical dynamic and, perhaps, angst over the United States’ place in the world. In the Pew and Chicago Council polls, younger adults are significantly more positively disposed toward China, evidence of a generational shift.

“Younger people have known China as a superpower,” Ms. Silver, the Pew researcher, said. Older generations, by contrast, are more likely to associate China with the developing world, Communism and the Tiananmen Square massacre of 1989, she said.

Younger people may also be more aware of China’s technological innovations and cultural exports, as evidenced by the “Chinamaxxing” trends ricocheting around the internet. That awareness comes in contrast to a sense of a decline in the United States’ global standing: 62 percent of Americans say the country is respected less in the world today than it was 10 years ago, according to the Chicago Council.

“You see fears of what’s happening to America be refracted through assessments of China,” said Nick Zeller, a scholar at the Carter Center in Atlanta who tracks how China and the United States perceive each other. “This positive assessment toward China has more to do with American political tumult domestically than it does China itself.”

item.title: St. Paul Police Chief Sues Mayor, Accusing Her of Sexual Harassment
item.description:
The police chief in St. Paul, Minn., sued Mayor Kaohly Her on Wednesday, accusing her of pursuing an intimate relationship while engaging in a monthslong pattern of unprofessional conduct, sexual harassment and retaliation.

The lawsuit in state court by the police chief, Axel Henry, represented a stark escalation of claims he made in a complaint last spring. It describes in greater detail what Mr. Henry says were inappropriate remarks, touching and pranks that severely strained the relationship between the mayor of a major American city and one of her top subordinates.

In one incident, the lawsuit says, Ms. Her placed her hand near Chief Henry’s groin during a meeting. In another, it says, Ms. Her removed personal photographs from Chief Henry’s office and replaced them with altered images depicting him and other officers posing as bodybuilders and as members of a boy band. The mayor’s behavior led one deputy police chief to retire early, the lawsuit says.

The lawsuit was filed five days after St. Paul’s top human resources official had announced that an independent review found that Ms. Her had treated employees in an “offensive and inappropriate way” and created an “uncomfortable work environment.” But the city’s summary of the investigation said it did not substantiate claims that Ms. Her sexually harassed colleagues.

In a statement on Wednesday, Ms. Her apologized for “any discomfort” and acknowledged that at times she “became too informal in my communications and crossed lines that are not consistent with the standards” for St. Paul municipal employees.

The mayor, who has been in office since January, said she had not yet read the full investigation, but was relieved that the summary did not find she had sexually harassed employees. The city has not released the report, which was written by a law firm.

Ms. Her, the daughter of Laotian refugees, was a state legislator and a top official in the city of St. Paul before running for mayor. She was elected as the first female mayor last year in an upset of an incumbent who had appointed Chief Henry to a six-year term in 2022.

Chief Henry, who leads a force of about 800 officers and civilians, declined to be interviewed on Wednesday.

In the 70-page lawsuit, Chief Henry, a 28-year veteran of the department, said that he filed his initial complaint last spring so that others on the force would not face harassment.

item.title: White House Backtracks on Plan to Exert New Control Over N.I.H. Grants
item.description:
The White House has backed away from a plan to issue an executive order that would subject billions of dollars in federal health and biomedical research spending to heightened political scrutiny, according to four people familiar with the situation.

The proposed directive would have established a commission with the power to block government research grants if the money supported work in areas that did not align with President Trump’s political agenda. The plan was discussed in a White House meeting on Friday, and some on Capitol Hill had expected Mr. Trump to issue the order as soon as this week.

But fierce opposition from both Democrats and Republicans in Congress forced the White House to recalibrate this week, according to some of the people familiar with the discussions, who described private conversations on the condition of anonymity. Nevertheless, they said, officials do not appear to have totally abandoned their desire to tighten their grip over federal research spending,

The White House, its Office of Management and Budget and the National Institutes of Health either did not respond to requests for comment, or declined to comment. The status of the order was reported earlier by Semafor.

At the heart of the matter is the N.I.H., the nation’s largest research agency, which disburses much of its $48 billion annual budget to researchers who study cancer, infectious diseases and other health priorities.

What you should know about anonymous sources. The Times makes a careful decision any time it shields the identity of a source. The information the source supplies must be newsworthy, credible and give readers genuine insight.

Historically, the N.I.H. has awarded these grants based on scientific merit after a rigorous review by experts in the relevant fields. But under Mr. Trump, political appointees have exerted extraordinary control over the grant-making process in a bid to eliminate spending seen as “woke,” and to exert pressure on Harvard University and other elite universities that the president accuses of antisemitism and liberal indoctrination.

The administration froze or cut more than 5,700 N.I.H. grants worth a total of $15 billion since Mr. Trump returned to the White House, although roughly 4,500 have been restored, some as a result of lawsuits, according to Grant Witness, a website run by research scientists. Researchers say the disruptions have created havoc in their labs.

Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, the N.I.H. director, has issued new guidelines for grant-making in an effort to carry out the president’s wishes, including his opposition to diversity, equity and inclusion programs. Last year, Dr. Bhattacharya co-wrote an opinion essay in The Spectator, titled “How We Cured DEI at the National Institutes of Health.”

But Mr. Trump and his budget director, Russell T. Vought, did not think the N.I.H. had gone far enough.

Tensions between them erupted during a highly fractious meeting on Friday, where Mr. Vought accused Mr. Bhattacharya of funding projects in conflict with the president’s past directives, including one issued on his first day in office prohibiting federal funding for D.E.I.-related programs.

News of the fiery session, which leaked over the weekend and was reported by various outlets, including The New York Times, created a bipartisan uproar on Capitol Hill. Congress, generally supportive of medical research, has previously refused Mr. Trump’s requests to cut N.I.H. spending.

Senator Susan Collins, Republican of Maine, who oversees the chamber’s appropriations committee, sent a letter to Mr. Vought and Dr. Bhattacharya warning that a new commission would “undermine” congressional intent and the pursuit of good science.

Her Democratic counterpart on the committee, Senator Patty Murray of Washington, separately accused Mr. Trump of trying to appoint a “panel of lackeys” whose primary task would be to help the president “settle a score.”

By Tuesday, several people familiar with the situation said, the O.M.B. and N.I.H. directors — who clashed so bitterly earlier in the year that at one point Mr. Vought refused to meet with Dr. Bhattacharya — were trying to forge a compromise. The goal, one of those people said, was to ensure that federal funding for biomedical research aligned with Mr. Trump’s priorities, while at the same time reducing political meddling in grant decisions.

Given those efforts, and the pressure from Congress, the White House retreated from its plan to sign the executive order as soon as this week, according to three people familiar with the matter.

It is unclear if the administration plans to revive the matter later through another directive. Since returning to office, the president has tried to block or revoke billions of dollars in congressionally approved research spending, often provoking ire on Capitol Hill and in federal courts.

Mr. Trump’s D.E.I. order had a far-reaching effect on longstanding N.I.H. work on health disparities, including populations and communities that are predisposed to certain diseases. Dr. Bhattacharya himself has conducted federally funded health disparities research.

Earlier this year, the president also tried to broaden his political litmus test to apply to a fuller roster of federal grant programs, including money that aids state and local governments. But that idea was met with vigorous opposition, particularly in Congress, which voted to block the White House from finalizing those rules.

Carolyn Y. Johnson and Michael C. Bender contributed reporting.

item.title: Paul LePage, a Trump Ally, Says a Family Member Is Being Deported
item.description:
Paul LePage, a former Maine governor and early supporter of President Trump who is now running for Congress, said during a campaign event this week that his son’s father-in-law is being wrongfully deported because of his country of origin.

“My son’s wife’s dad is here legally,” Mr. LePage said at a news conference after being endorsed by a police union. “But he’s being deported because he came from a country that’s not liked by certain people in Washington. That’s not right.”

The former governor made sweeping statements while in office that denigrated asylum seekers, while enacting policies that curtailed refugee resettlement and state benefits for many migrants. He touted that record in an ad this week, but also emphasized that he supports “legal, but not illegal, immigration.”

He said his son’s father-in-law has a work permit and “should be allowed to stay.” His campaign declined to provide further details about the case on Wednesday, and the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Work permits are typically granted to migrants who do not have visas or green cards, such as those with Temporary Protected Status, a legal status for immigrants from troubled countries. Mr. Trump has rescinded it for hundreds of thousands of residents, including migrants from Afghanistan, Haiti and Venezuela.

Mr. LePage cited his in-law when responding to a question from a Portland Press Herald reporter about whether the arrest of immigrants without criminal records is “making Maine safe.” Maine is one of several states where Immigration and Customs Enforcement has sent a surge of agents this year as part of Mr. Trump’s mass deportation efforts.

Mr. LePage replied that anyone in the U.S. illegally has “broken the law,” but said he believes enforcement actions should prioritize “people in the gangs and criminals,” because “not everybody that’s here is illegal.” He expressed frustration with immigration law, which he said “needs to be fixed.”

Mr. LePage is running for a House district in northern Maine against Matt Dunlap, a progressive state auditor, for the seat held by retiring Representative Jared Golden, a moderate Democrat.

Mr. Dunlap said the former governor was “trying to run from his record” on immigration. Mr. Dunlap has rejected calls to abolish ICE, but says the agency needs stronger oversight.

“Paul LePage is no friend to immigrants or their families,” the Democrat said in a statement. “He spent eight years demonizing them as governor, and he welcomed ICE’s overreach into Maine.”

An ICE agent fatally shot an unarmed Colombian man in Biddeford, Maine, this summer, sparking widespread protests and roiling state politics. The administration has not said whether the man, Johan Sebastian Durán Guerrero, 25, was the target of an enforcement operation, but defended the officer who opened fire.

Mr. LePage’s immigration ad released this week addresses voters in both English and French, which is still spoken by a significant segment of Maine residents of French Canadian heritage.

“Immigration built our nation,” Mr. LePage says in the ad, noting that French was his first language. He then touts his record as governor, saying he “ended Maine as an illegal immigration sanctuary state, cut off welfare to illegal immigrants, and made sure taxpayer dollars went to Mainers.”

item.title: Michigan Governor Orders Inquiry After ICE Pursuit Ends in Fatal Crash
item.description:
Gov. Gretchen Whitmer of Michigan, a Democrat, has ordered a state investigation after a man who was being pursued by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents died in a car crash last weekend in Grand Rapids.

The man was identified by officials as Mario David Coronado Juarez, an immigrant from Guatemala. Mr. Juarez’s immigration status was not immediately clear.

“Given the circumstances of this incident, the governor has directed the Michigan State Police to conduct an independent review of the law enforcement actions surrounding this situation in coordination with the Grand Rapids Police Department’s investigation,” Kaylie Hanson, a spokeswoman for Ms. Whitmer, said in a statement.

Elected officials and advocates for immigrants in Michigan have decried Mr. Coronado Juarez’s death, asking how a routine immigration stop could have resulted in a fatal crash. Mr. Coronado Juarez was the only occupant of the car, the authorities said, which hit a tree and caught fire.

The pursuit in Michigan was the latest example of ICE activity around the country ending in injury or death. In Austin, Texas, this week, an immigration agent shot an immigrant from Venezuela in his vehicle. That man, Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, was hospitalized and then released into ICE custody.

In Evanston, Ill., a suburb of Chicago, a U.S. citizen was left with injuries to his head, neck and teeth after he was mistakenly detained by immigration agents last weekend, according to the local police.

In July, a 28-year-old man running from immigration agents at a gas station in St. Augustine, Fla., was struck and killed by a tractor-trailer. Days before that, an immigration agent in Biddeford, Maine, shot and killed a man in a car. Also in early July, an ICE agent fatally shot a Mexican immigrant, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, during a traffic stop in Houston.

Activists in Grand Rapids said that Mr. Coronado Juarez’s death last weekend underscored their growing fears of an intensified crackdown by immigration agents. At a news conference on Tuesday, residents of Grand Rapids said that Mr. Coronado Juarez was a construction worker with family members in Guatemala who wanted answers about the circumstances of his death.

United States Representative Hillary Scholten, a Democrat who represents Grand Rapids, said that she had requested information from ICE about the incident, including what the purpose of the stop was, if Mr. Coronado Juarez was the target of an investigation and whether agents were wearing body cameras.

“No traffic stop should end with a fatality,” she said in a statement. “Something went wrong, and we need to know what and how.”

The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to an email seeking comment.

Robert S. Womack, a commissioner in Kent County, Mich., which includes Grand Rapids, called the death of Mr. Coronado Juarez “a profound human tragedy that demands rigorous accountability, transparency from both local and federal agencies.”

On Tuesday, demonstrators disrupted a Grand Rapids City Commission meeting to protest Mr. Coronado Juarez’s death, chanting “abolish ICE” and asking that Grand Rapids be declared a sanctuary city.
